newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy social security says '97 budget to overshoot.
newsitem.headline: Italy social security says '97 budget to overshoot.

text.p: Italian social security body INPs said in a statement on Monday that its projected 1997 deficit looked set to overshoot 1996 levels by around 10 trillion lire because of an expected jump in pensions spending.
It said that its deficit was on course to hit 27 trillion lire next year from around 17 trillion in 1996.
However it added that if the 1997 budget, which is currently being examined by parliament, was approved in its present form, the deficit would be contained to 21 trillion lire.
INPs predicted it would need 83.3 trillion lire next year to cover its various outgoings -- mostly made up of pensions and unemployment payouts.

It said the anticipated climb in pensions spending was largely due to a wave of people who want to retire, but whose bid to draw state benefit has been blocked up until now by a Treasury bid to hold back early retirements.
After months of waiting, a window of opportunity for people seeking early retirement is due to open next year. INPS predicted some 350,000 people would seize the chance.
However it said the government had taken the projected increase in spending into account when it drew up the budget.

The 1997 financial package is due to go before the full Chamber of Deputies (lower house of parliament) later this week, with a final vote on the budget due there by November 17. After that it goes to the Senate (upper house) for ratification.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government has appeared increasingly anxious in recent days over pensions spending and both Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi and Deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni have called for a planned review of a 1995 pension reform to be brought forward a year to 1997.

Both the unions and the hard left Communist Refoundation, which supports the government in parliament, have rejected the request, arguing that the first review of the reform must go ahead, as planned, in 1998. -- Rome newsroom +396 6782501
